hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? if someone asked you right now, “where are you in your life?”, would you know what to say?
options: that’s honest. this question is very old. listen.
so did the first person ever asked. listen.

steps.line: In the garden, the first man and woman ate from the one tree they were told to leave alone. The text never says apple. Just fruit.
Their eyes were opened. They sewed fig leaves together, and when they heard God in the garden in the cool of the day, they hid among the trees.
And God called to the man, “Where art thou?” In Hebrew, it’s one word: ayekah.

steps.q: God knows exactly where the man is. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, asks: so why ask?
o: To catch him in a lie
To start a conversation, not a sentence
To give the woman time to come out
steps.why: Rashi says God opened gently, so the man wouldn’t be too frightened to answer. A rabbi in a Russian prison will give another answer soon.

steps.q: The man is asked where he is. What do you think he does?
o: Says he was scared, then blames her
steps.why: He said he was afraid, then pointed at the woman. And she pointed at the snake.

steps.line: “I heard Thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid,” he said. Then he pointed: the woman gave me the fruit. And she pointed at the snake.

steps.q: The man says he was afraid, then blames someone. Why does the blame matter?
o: He still hasn’t really said where he is
It proves the woman was guilty
steps.why: He answered the question, and dodged it at the same time. Blame is another place to hide.

steps.line: Long after, in a Russian prison, an official asked a jailed rabbi, Shneur Zalman: “If God knows everything, why ask Adam where he is?”
steps.label: a Hasidic story

steps.line: The rabbi answered: in every age, God calls to every person, “Where are you in your world? So many years of your life have passed. Where are you?”
steps.label: a Hasidic story

steps.q: In the telling, the rabbi didn’t just say “so many years.” He named a number. Whose age was it?
o: Adam’s, when he left the garden
The rabbi’s, on the day he was jailed
steps.why: He said “forty-six years have passed,” and the official was forty-six. Shaken, the man saw that the question was for him.

steps.line: Today, many Jews hear ayekah not as a trap but as a door left open: come out, and say where you are.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. god obviously knows where the man is. so one answer in jewish teaching is that the question isn’t for god. it’s for the man: a door left open.
and look what he does with the door. he answers, then points. the first question, and the first blame, passed along like a hot plate. the question is still waiting for a straight answer.

steps.q: If the question is really for us, what would a straight answer to ayekah sound like?
o: “Here I am, and here’s what I did.”
steps.why: Here I am, hineni in Hebrew, is what Abraham and Moses say when God calls them. No hiding, no pointing.

today.say: tonight, ask yourself the one-word question: ayekah, where am i? answer in one honest sentence, no blame, no excuses. write it down if you like.
options: one honest sentence. that’s the door, open.
that’s honest too. the question will wait for you.

card.keepWhy: Where are you? Answer without blame.
